product.description: A hand-built, 3D-printed mechanical robot with a gear train and a long vertical spring-loaded leg, plus two V-shaped linkage arms ending in ball tips. A green circuit board and a 9V battery are mounted on one side and wired to the motor, suggesting a jumping or hopping prototype. A DIY robotic mechanism built around a gray 3D-printed C-shaped frame holding an SG92R micro servo, N20 gear motors with encoder boards, and large printed spur gears meshing with a curved rack. It is wired with twisted multicolor cables and mounted on a spring-loaded threaded rod, with a green prototype PCB at one side. A hand-built robot with a 3D-printed dark frame, a custom green PCB carrying a Teensy and two motor driver boards, and a long spring-wrapped vertical leg ending in a round foot. Two splayed 3D-printed arms with rounded tips extend outward, and a cylindrical battery pack is mounted on the left side with loose wiring throughout.

assembly.summary: A Teensy on a custom carrier PCB drives two N20 encoder gear motors through two H-bridge driver boards, plus an SG92R servo and a brass gear motor, to move a 3D-printed gear train and curved rack that load and release a spring-wrapped threaded-rod leg. Encoder feedback closes the position loop on the motors, and the servo likely adjusts the splayed linkage arms or a latch (assumption from photos). A battery supplies the motors and a regulated 5V rail supplies the logic.

build_steps: Print the frame, gears, rack and arms, then clean them and test-fit the bearings and shafts with a craft knife and files.
Press pinions onto the motor shafts and screw the N20 motors, brass motor and servo into the frame with M3/M2 screws and a hex key.
Solder headers and drivers to the carrier PCB, fit the 5V regulator and add a power switch.
Crimp or solder JST-SH cables for encoders and motors, then check polarity with a multimeter.
Mount the Teensy and carrier PCB on the frame with standoffs, and secure the battery with foam tape and cable ties.
Assemble the threaded rod, springs and foot, then retain them with nuts and thread-lock.
Bench-test each motor at low PWM with the leg unloaded, and verify encoder counts, direction and servo travel.
Tune the gear and rack mesh, then run the spring-load and release cycle slowly before attempting hops.

risks: A 9V battery has high internal resistance and low capacity, so motor stall or servo spikes can brown out the Teensy. Use a LiPo or separate rails.
DRV8833/TB6612 breakouts have current limits of about 1.2-1.5A, which may be exceeded at stall.
Printed gears and the rack can strip or wear under spring-loaded shock. Use thicker nylon or metal pinions.
Loose wiring near the moving gears and leg can snag or fatigue at solder joints.
